passage:
Monday: Maria was hanging clothes on the balcony in Goa when a peg dropped. Gargi toddled over, picked it up and held it high until Maria took it.
Wednesday: Maria came in with shopping bags in both hands. Gargi ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.
Saturday: Maria's spoon clattered off the table. Before anyone spoke, Gargi fetched it and handed it up, not waiting for a thank-you.

qa.q: What did Gargi do on Wednesday when Maria came in with shopping bags?
qa.a: She ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.

qa.q: Why do you think Gargi picks things up without being asked?
qa.a: Gargi seems caring and eager to help when Maria needs something, since Gargi does it without being asked or waiting for thanks.

qa.q: How can Maria encourage Gargi's helping without turning it into a reward game?
qa.a: She can warmly say what Gargi did, like "You opened the door for me," rather than offering sweets for each help.

qa.q: What would change if Maria only praised Gargi when she had asked her to help?
qa.a: Gargi might start helping only on request, and her natural, unasked kindness could fade.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items and helping without prompt or reward over several days.

passage: In their Bengaluru flat, Lakshmi Paati bent over the newspaper and her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa. She sighed and began to lower herself to her knees. Nitin, two, dropped his toy truck, crawled flat under the sofa and came out holding the glasses by one arm. He pushed them into her hand. When her pen rolled off the table a moment later, he grabbed that too, then went straight back to his truck.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi Paati's glasses slide?
qa.a: Her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa.

qa.q: What might Nitin have noticed that made him drop his truck?
qa.a: He probably saw Paati sigh and start to kneel, and seemed to understand she needed help reaching the glasses.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi Paati respond to Nitin's help?
qa.a: She could thank him simply and warmly so he knows his help mattered, without making a fuss or offering a treat.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Paati see Nitin crawling under the sofa for her?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and touched that such a small child noticed her struggle and helped on his own. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously fetching dropped items for an elder without being asked.

passage:
"Oops, my keys!" Sunaina said as they hit the floor by the door.
Uday, who was pulling on one sandal, dropped it and waddled over. "Keys!"
"Oh, you got them?"
"Here, Mummy." He held them up with both hands.
"Thank you, Uday."
He was already back at his sandal. A minute later her dupatta slipped off her shoulder. Uday tugged the end and lifted it up to her.
"Look at you, noticing everything," she laughed.

qa.q: What was Uday doing when the keys fell?
qa.a: He was pulling on one sandal by the door.

qa.q: What does Uday going straight back to his sandal suggest about why he helped?
qa.a: It suggests he was simply happy to help rather than hoping for praise, since he went straight back without waiting for more thanks.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say next time to encourage this kind of help?
qa.a: She could name exactly what he did, such as "You picked up my keys," so he sees how his help made a difference.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Uday lifts her dupatta up to her?
qa.a: She would probably feel amused and warm, surprised at how quickly he notices small things she needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items for his mother without prompt or reward.

passage:
Playgroup note from Irfan Sir
Today Alka, who is two and a half, did something sweet. When a friend's crayon box fell and scattered, Alka went straight over, picked up every crayon and dropped them back in, one by one. Nobody asked her. Later she handed me my keys when they slipped off the table. 👍 I just said, 'Thank you, Alka,' and she went back to her puzzle.

qa.q: What did Alka hand to Irfan Sir later?
qa.a: She handed him his keys when they slipped off the table.

qa.q: What does Alka going back to her puzzle after being thanked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she helped because she wanted to, not to get praise or a reward.

qa.q: What did Irfan Sir do well in his response?
qa.a: He thanked her simply without making a big fuss or giving a prize, which keeps the helping her own choice.

qa.q: How might the friend whose crayons fell see Alka?
qa.a: The friend may feel looked after and more likely to see Alka as kind and friendly.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously helping by picking up dropped items without being asked.

passage: By the village well, Kishore Dada was washing his face, his gamchha draped on the stone edge. A gust blew it into the dust. Before he could bend, little Devika toddled over, grabbed the cloth in both fists and held it up to him, beaming. 'Dada, lo!' Nobody had told her to. He took it, laughed, and ruffled her hair. She was already running back to chase the hens.

qa.q: What did the gust blow into the dust?
qa.a: It blew Kishore Dada's gamchha off the stone edge into the dust.

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel about helping Dada?
qa.a: She seemed happy and eager, beaming as she held the cloth up to him without anyone asking.

qa.q: How could adults encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: They can notice it warmly, as Dada did with a laugh, without turning it into a task or a reward.

qa.q: How does Kishore Dada see what Devika did?
qa.a: He seems touched and amused that such a small child noticed and helped him on her own.

grounding: Shows a toddler assisting an elder without prompt or reward, set in an Indian village.
